fields.title: Obod: Growth Stalled, Proposal to Target Chains
fields.summary: Sales have hit a ceiling, and management wants to target a larger segment. Decide where the ceiling actually is.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you propose at the board meeting and based on what calculation?
fields.brief/company: Obod is a fictional booking and job tracking service for independent auto repair shops with 2–8 bays. 310 customers, average bill of 18 thousand per month.
fields.brief/context: The number of customers has barely grown for six months. The commercial director proposes targeting auto repair chains with 20+ bays: the average bill there is three times higher. He wants to move the sales team to the new segment starting next month. You have one week before the decision.
fields.brief/objective: Understand where growth has actually stalled and propose what to do.
fields.brief/constraints: Sales team of three. Development team of four, available from the middle of the quarter.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you will propose at the board meeting and explain the calculation.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Calculate the segment bottom-up before changing it
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A higher average bill doesn't mean a larger segment: the number of customers is multiplied by the bill, and the tempting market often turns out to be dozens of times smaller than the current one. When growth stops, first check if acquisition equals churn—because if it does, the ceiling is internal, not external, and usually costs a week of development to fix, not a change of strategy.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
There are about 27,000 independent auto repair shops with 2–8 bays in the country. According to an industry portal, about 35% use some software, while the rest keep records in notebooks and messengers.

Your customers: 310. Average bill: 18 thousand/month.

A sales team of three closes 8 deals a month, with a sales cycle of three weeks. For the last six months, the number of closed deals equals churn: churn is 2.5% per month.

With 27,000 shops and an 18 thousand bill, the addressable segment is around 5.8 billion per year. You occupy 67 million of it, which is just over one percent.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
There are about 240 auto repair chains with 20+ bays in the country.

The commercial director estimates the average bill at 55 thousand/month. With 240 chains, the entire segment is about 158 million per year, which is 36 times smaller than the current one.

In an independent shop, the owner (who is often also the head mechanic) makes the decision: one conversation, three-week cycle.

In a chain, three people decide: the COO, IT, and finance. Based on two past conversations, the cycle was over six months, and both times the deal fell through—they required integration with their accounting system and a dedicated manager.

The team has no experience with implementations for chains.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Churn of 2.5% per month is about 8 customers, exactly the same number as new acquisitions.

Support analyzed 24 churned customers over the quarter: 15 stopped using the service in the first two months, 9 left later.

Of the 15 early churns: 11 never set up their job list and prices—this needs to be done once, manually, and takes several hours.

Uploading a price list from a file is a one-week development task that has been sitting in the backlog for four months.

Among the 9 late churns, the reasons vary with no repeating pattern.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
The demo is 40 minutes going through sections on a demo environment with placeholder jobs like 'Oil Change', 'Job 2'.

The salesperson with the best conversion rate does things differently: before the meeting, he asks how many cars they service per day and where they lose time, then shows a single scenario—booking a customer and handing the car over to the mechanic.

His demo-to-deal conversion rate is 41% compared to 22% for the other two. No one has adopted this format: 'everyone has their own style.'

There are currently no discounts. Price was never mentioned in any of the 24 churn analyses.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Calculate both segments bottom-up and fix retention
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Show that the chain segment is several times smaller than the current one, that growth is bottlenecked by churn and sales methodology, and dedicate the quarter to price list uploads and adopting the successful demo format.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The bottom-up calculation makes an impact: 240 chains × 55 thousand is 158 million per year, compared to 5.8 billion in the current segment where you occupy one percent. The board agrees not to pivot sales.
Price list upload is released in a week. The share of customers setting up their job list in the first month grows from 46% to 78%; early churn drops by half over the quarter.
The demo format is analyzed in a team meeting, and a pre-meeting question becomes mandatory. Conversion for the two lagging salespeople grows from 22% to 31% in two months.
The number of customers grows from 310 to 372 over the quarter—for the first time in six months.
Trade-off: you publicly opposed the commercial director, and the chain segment remains unexplored.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The average bill is three times higher, and the current segment is exhausted. Move the three salespeople to chains starting next month.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Zero deals close in the first three months: the sales cycle for chains is six months or longer, and requirements like integration with their accounting system and a dedicated manager are not met.
Sales in the current segment stop, and churn remains at 2.5%: the number of customers drops from 310 to 287.
A quarter later, the segment is calculated bottom-up: 240 chains × 55 thousand is 158 million per year, 36 times smaller than the segment you left.
Trade-off: you changed segments based on the average bill size without calculating how many customers actually exist in it.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: There are 27,000 shops in the segment, and you have 310. Hire three more salespeople and double the deal flow.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Hiring and training take two months. Deal flow grows from 8 to 14 per month.
The number of customers grows slower than expected: churn remains at 2.5%, and the new salespeople use the overview demo format with a conversion rate of around 20%.
In six months, the customer count reaches 358 instead of the projected 400+, and acquisition cost rises.
Upon review, you realize that a week of development for price list uploads would have yielded a comparable increase without increasing expenses.
Trade-off: you correctly identified that the ceiling was in the channel, but started pouring water into a leaky bucket.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Lower the price for the remaining market
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: 65% of the segment work in notebooks—18 thousand is likely too expensive for them. Lower the price and capture the non-automated market.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The price is reduced by 30%. New deal flow grows from 8 to 11 per month, but revenue drops.
Early churn remains unchanged: the same 11 out of 15 do not set up their job list. More people sign up, and just as many leave in the first two months.
Price was never mentioned in any of the 24 churn analyses—which was known before making the decision.
Trade-off: you assumed the reluctance to automate was due to price without verifying it, and paid with your margin.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: An objection was mistaken for a feature debate rather than an expressed risk
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Failing to distinguish between users and decision-makers
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: The demo focuses on product sections rather than the customer's problem
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Showing only the happy path, without any edge cases
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Segment size was calculated top-down as a percentage of a large report
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Looking for a growth ceiling in the market without checking the sales methodology
